newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen lower at open, Greenspan to speak.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen lower at open, Greenspan to speak.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open lower Wednesday as Wall Street once again trades in the shadow of testimony by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Grenspan.
Greenspan will deliver the second phase of his semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress today; the first part sent markets tumbling last week.

"The testimony will be the main focus of the day. Will he continue to pour cold water on the market?" said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "I think he will reiterate what he said last week."
Greenspan put financial markets on a state of high alert last week with blunt warnings on stock prices and interest rates during the first phase of his testimony.
However, during an unrelated appearance Tuesday before the U.S. House of Representatives' Budget Committee, Greenspan denied his comments were aimed at affecting the market.

"It is his style to say something, retreat and then come back and reinforce the original statement," Cardillo said. "I think he will continue to prepare the market for an interest rate hike. The question remains whether he will pull the trigger sooner or later."
Hildegard Zagorski, analyst at Prudential Securities, said the market was likely to head lower at the open.
"I am looking for a slightly lower opening, but the market will just hang around and not do much of anything until it sees whether Greenspan has any more bombshells," she said.
Cardillo said that investors were also cautious ahead of this Friday's February employment report, a statistic carefully watched by the Federal Reserve.
"If we get a substantial hike in hourly wages, anything above 0.7 percent, we could see a pre-emptive strike by the Fed as early as Friday," he said.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 291.27 points, or 1.57 percent, at 18,273.51.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 12.5 points at 4345.2.
U.S. shares were little changed in quiet trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the second phase of Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
The dollar was mixed in Tokyo and off its highs. It was firmer against the mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly lower, with the long bond down 5/32 to yield 6.88 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that analysts warn that the most aggressive lenders -- the so-called subprime lenders, who target borrowers with troubled credit histories -- are leading bigger banks, like Citicorp and Chase Manhattan Corp, to loosen their home-lending standards as well.

The New York Times' Market Place writes that analysts seem to like the stocks of scrap metal recyclers and of service companies that turn steel into usable parts, but Wall Street is divided on old-time steelmakers like USX-U.S. Steel Group.
